scoreNote: Strong-adequate (4.5): grants that like-minded people teach us something, then argues opposing views teach more; two developed examples with analysis, controlled prose on a memorable First and Second skeleton.

sentences.text: Most of us enjoy the company of people who already think the way we do.
Some people argue that we can learn much more from people whose views we share than from those whose views contradict our own.
I agree that like-minded people can teach us something, but I believe we usually learn more from those who disagree.

sections.role: Body 1 — What shared views can teach

sentences.text: First, people who share our views can certainly help us learn.
They can strengthen our understanding by adding fresh facts to ideas we already accept.
For example, colleagues who agree on a project can build steadily on one another's work.
This shows that agreement can offer a comfortable and productive place to learn.
Working with allies also gives us the confidence to develop our ideas more boldly.
Shared understanding can make hard learning feel encouraging rather than frightening.
To this extent, like-minded people do have something to teach us.

sections.role: Body 2 — Why opposing views teach more

sentences.text: Second, however, we usually learn the most from people whose views oppose our own.
Those who disagree force us to defend our beliefs and to face their hidden weaknesses.
Consider how a sharp opponent can expose a flaw in our argument that no friend would mention.
Such challenges drive us to think harder and to understand a question far more deeply.
People who merely agree with us, by contrast, rarely teach us anything truly new.
Facing opposing views also helps us see the world as other people genuinely see it.
Disagreement, handled with respect, is therefore one of our finest teachers.
In conclusion, people who share our views can add to what we already understand.
But we usually grow more by wrestling with those who think very differently.
The richest learning springs not from easy agreement but from honest, respectful disagreement.
